changes.current_line: Support plans with tiered response times, up to 24/7 coverage.
changes.change: For operations deciders (COO-level) at businesses whose revenue concentrates in peak events: lead with a person, not a plan level. Suggested wording: "A name, not a queue. You get a named owner on our side, someone who picks up, and a clear escalation path for your biggest days." Keep tiers and response times as backup detail only. Confirm with support and solutions engineering what named-contact commitment we can actually make before using it.
changes.why: Jordan walked Halima through the tiers and response times, and she dismissed them as "a queue with a faster timer" because she was asking for a named person who picks up, never for "support."

changes.change: New proof asset for prospects whose revenue concentrates in spikes, such as on-sales: a written peak-event readiness plan showing "what we do on an on-sale morning". It should name the roles watching, who the customer calls, the escalation path, and the minute-by-minute response when something fails. Offer it to the decider before the decision meeting. Only state event-day coverage we have confirmed we can deliver.
changes.why: Halima wanted to see this on paper and we had nothing to show ("We don't have that as a thing"), while the competitor stated on-call coverage for every major on-sale.

changes.change: For operations buyers switching after a payments incident, open with the customer's own frame: "I don't buy uptime, I buy what happens when it's down." Lead with what happens in the first minutes of a failure and who responds. Keep the developer story, load test, and uptime history for the CTO track, not as the decider-level opener.
changes.why: The load test went great with the CTO's team but drew one word from Halima, "good.", and her own line shows she valued incident response over uptime proof.

changes.current_line: Trusted by leading businesses; see our customer stories.
changes.change: For peak-event and incident-driven deals: replace logo proof with a reference person, a customer who can describe how our team picked up during a real incident. Offer the reference conversation directly to the decider. This requires identifying a customer willing to speak to an incident before it can be used.
changes.why: Jordan's own diagnosis was "I had logos. I didn't have a person." That is a poor fit for a decider whose standard was "A name, not a queue."
